provenance.other: “voice of the people” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Samuel 8:7. This is not the KJV’s ordinary way of saying popular consent: within 1 Samuel 8 itself the idiom is “their voice” (8:9, 8:22) and “the voice of Samuel” (8:19), and 1 Samuel 12:1 has “your voice”. The definite, collective form the Book of Mormon adopts as the name of its constitution exists once in the English Bible.
provenance.significance: Recover the rest of the verse and the borrowing turns on its author. The KJV’s one authorisation to hearken to the voice of the people is God conceding a rejection of himself: “they have not rejected thee, but they have rejected me, that I should not reign over them.” Mosiah takes that phrase, which in its own context licenses a monarchy God did not want, and makes it the instrument for abolishing monarchy — and then at 29:12 gives the reason in the terms of the same episode, that it is better to be judged of God than of man. The chapter is not quoting 1 Samuel 8 so much as reversing it: the people ask for a king (29:2), the ruler sends a written warning about what a king does (29:22-23, which is the office of Samuel’s “manner of the king”), and at 29:37 they are convinced, where Israel refused. Mosiah keeps the phrase and cancels the outcome. The counter-current is 29:27, where the voice of the people may itself “choose iniquity” — which is what 1 Samuel 8 records it doing.

29:2.note: “And it came to pass that the voice of the people came, saying: We are desirous that Aaron, thy son, should be our king.” The situation is 1 Samuel 8’s to the detail — a people petitioning an ageing ruler for a king to be drawn from his own sons — and the noun phrase that carries it exists in exactly one KJV verse, the verse in which God tells Samuel to give in. The phrase is first adjudicated in this book at Mosiah 7:9, where Limhi uses it of Zeniff’s accession, and by ADJUDICATING §4 a repeat inside one book is normally discharged in the exclusion register. The row is written out again here because this is not the formula recurring: it is the phrase returning to the scene it came from, with the petition, the sons, the written protest and the people’s answer all present, and because from this verse forward it is the name of a form of government rather than a description of an accession. Wilson’s ruling is wanted on whether a case of that kind takes a second row or an exclusion; the argument at 7:9 is not restated here, only extended.
29:2.text: And the LORD said unto Samuel, Hearken unto the voice of the people in all that they say unto thee: for they have not rejected thee, but they have rejected me, that I should not reign over them.

provenance.route: Judges 8:22-23 and Judges 9 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.significance: Judges 8:22-23 is the KJV’s one scene of a deliverer refusing an offered crown for himself and for his son, and its stated ground — “the LORD shall rule over you” — is the ground Mosiah gives at 29:12. What makes the parallel worth writing is the sequel. Judges 9 is what happens when one son does not refuse: Abimelech draws the men of Shechem after him, slays his seventy brethren on one stone, and the kingdom he seizes ends in civil war. Mosiah 29:7-9 states that sequel as a fear rather than a history — a son who will “turn to be angry, and draw away a part of this people after him”, causing “wars and contentions” and “shedding much blood” — and 29:8’s odd insistence that “we have no right to destroy my son” is the Abimelech remedy explicitly declined. Gideon refuses and his son takes it anyway; Mosiah refuses on behalf of sons who have already refused, and closes the succession instead of trusting it.

29:3.note: Aaron has gone up to the land of Nephi and none of the sons of Mosiah will take the kingdom. No clause of Judges is reproduced, but the shape is exact and it is a shape the KJV supplies once: the household of a deliverer declining a crown the people have offered it. The reason for proposing it rather than passing over it is 29:7-9, where the chapter narrates the Abimelech aftermath as the danger it is legislating against — an angry son, a party drawn away, blood shed — without naming it.
29:3.whyNot: This is a link at the level of narrative form with almost no verbal contact; “rule over you” occurs in five KJV verses and Mosiah does not use it. A reader who declines typological arguments has nothing here to hold on to, and the succession crisis of 29:1-9 is adequately explained by the Book of Mormon’s own dynastic narrative without any Judges behind it.
29:3.text: And Gideon said unto them, I will not rule over you, neither shall my son rule over you: the LORD shall rule over you.

provenance.other: “have a king” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Samuel 8:19. The KJV’s usual constructions are “set a king over” (Deuteronomy 17:14-15), “make them a king” (1 Samuel 8:22) and “reign over us” (seven verses); the Book of Mormon uses the one form the Bible uses once, and uses it four times in this chapter.
provenance.significance: The KJV’s single “have a king” is a refusal: “Nevertheless the people refused to obey the voice of Samuel; and they said, Nay; but we will have a king over us.” Mosiah 29 is that verse run forward with the opposite result. The written word he sends is Samuel’s protest delivered a second time, and 29:37-38 reports the outcome 1 Samuel 8:19 denied: “they were convinced of the truth of his words; therefore they relinquished their desires for a king.” The borrowed phrase carries the refusal with it, which is why the chapter keeps repeating it — at 29:13 as the concession, at 29:16 as the verdict, and at 29:30 as the command “that ye have no king.”

29:5.note: “For ye are desirous to have a king.” Three ordinary words, but the collocation is a KJV singleton and it belongs to the one biblical scene this whole chapter is rewriting. Below Skousen’s sixteen-word threshold by a wide margin and not one of his passages; the case rests on rarity and on the density of 1 Samuel 8 contact across the chapter (see 29:2, 29:23, 29:40) rather than on length.
29:5.text: Nevertheless the people refused to obey the voice of Samuel; and they said, Nay; but we will have a king over us;

provenance.other: “lifted up above his brethren” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Deuteronomy 17:20, and “multiply to himself” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Deuteronomy 17:17. Neither string is reproduced; what is shared is their content.
provenance.significance: Deuteronomy 17:14-20 is the Torah’s law of the king, and its three prohibitions are the three things Mosiah is praised for not doing: his heart is not lifted up above his brethren (29:5, and 29:32’s “every man may enjoy his rights and privileges alike”), he did not multiply silver and gold to himself (29:40, “he had not exacted riches of them”), and he wrote out the law rather than ruling above it (17:18-19, and Mosiah’s “written word” at 29:4). The law of the king anticipates a king who will behave as Mosiah does; Mosiah’s conclusion is that no institution can guarantee it, which is 29:13 and 29:16 in a sentence.

29:5.note: “Behold, O ye my people, or my brethren, for I esteem you as such.” The self-correction is the point: a king addresses his people and immediately declines the relation the word implies. Deuteronomy 17:20’s one requirement of an Israelite king is that his heart be not lifted up above his brethren, and the KJV says that in exactly those words once. The wording is not reproduced and the argument is a conceptual one, offered under CONVENTIONS §0a as worth putting on the table because the law of the king governs the rest of the chapter whether or not this verse alludes to it.
29:5.whyNot: “Brethren” is the Book of Mormon’s standard address and appears in this position throughout the corpus; no distinctive wording of Deuteronomy 17 is present, and the sentiment is available from Mosiah 2:26, King Benjamin’s “I am as ye are”, without any Deuteronomy in the room.
29:5.text: That his heart be not lifted up above his brethren, and that he turn not aside from the commandment, to the right hand, or to the left: to the end that he may prolong his days in his kingdom, he, and his children, in the midst of Israel.

provenance.other: “draw away” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 20:30, where it governs the same preposition and the same construction: “to draw away disciples after them” against Mosiah’s “draw away a part of this people after him.” The pervert-word is in both sentences as well — Acts has “speaking perverse things”, and Mosiah 29:7 continues “perverting the way of the Lord”.
provenance.significance: Acts 20 is Paul’s farewell at Miletus, and its argument is that the schism to come will not be imported: “of your own selves shall men arise.” Mosiah 29 is a farewell of the same genre — a ruler who says at 29:11 that he will serve out the remainder of his days and who is dead by 29:46 — and the danger he names is likewise domestic, a son of his own house drawing a party after him. Borrowing the phrase brings the genre with it. It also brings the sequel: the formula recurs at Alma 2:3, where the first crisis of the reign of judges is a people “drawn away after the persuasions of Amlici”, a man who wants to be king. What Mosiah forecasts in Paul’s words happens to the system he is founding within three chapters.

29:7.note: “Who knoweth but what my son … should turn to be angry, and draw away a part of this people after him.” The verb is a KJV singleton, it is here with its own preposition and its own object-construction, and the perversion language of Acts 20:30 shows up in the next clause of the same Book of Mormon sentence. That is two independent points of contact on a phrase that occurs once in the English Bible, which is why this is high rather than moderate.
29:7.text: Also of your own selves shall men arise, speaking perverse things, to draw away disciples after them.

provenance.other: “destroy souls” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Ezekiel 22:27, and the same verse supplies the two clauses on either side of the Book of Mormon’s: “to shed blood, and to destroy souls, to get dishonest gain.” Mosiah 29:7 reads “the cause of shedding much blood … yea, and destroy the souls of much people”, and the third element arrives at 29:40 in the tyrant “who was seeking for gain”. mediation-check.py was run on this verse against Proverbs 1:16 and Romans 3:15 and returned a decisive call for both, which inspection shows to be an alignment artifact: the tool lost the phrase because Mosiah reads “destroy THE souls” and the intervening article broke its window. Ezekiel 22:27 is the only KJV verse that has the phrase at all, so there is nothing for the diff to mediate.
provenance.significance: Ezekiel 22:27 is an indictment of rulers as a class — “her princes in the midst thereof are like wolves ravening the prey” — and it is the one KJV verse that puts bloodshed, the destruction of souls, and the pursuit of gain into a single charge against them. Mosiah 29 distributes that charge across the chapter and then acquits the last king of every count of it (29:40). The prophetic indictment of princes becomes a constitutional argument: what Ezekiel says of the princes of Jerusalem, Mosiah says is what the office does to whoever holds it.

29:7.note: “Which would be the cause of shedding much blood … yea, and destroy the souls of much people.” Two words, but they are two words that occur together nowhere else in the KJV and they arrive with their neighbour clause attached. Proposed at moderate rather than high because the phrase is short and the sense (killing people) is the obvious one; the argument is the company it keeps.
29:7.whyNot: “Destroy” and “souls” are both common and their combination is not a difficult thing for an English writer to reach independently. Mosiah shows no other contact with Ezekiel 22, and the bloodshed language of the verse is the chapter’s own from 29:21 onward.
29:7.text: Her princes in the midst thereof are like wolves ravening the prey, to shed blood, and to destroy souls, to get dishonest gain.

provenance.route: Deuteronomy 1:13-17 (with Exodus 18:21-26) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “wise men” is in 42 KJV verses and cannot identify a source by itself. The distribution is the argument: of those 42, only Deuteronomy 1:13 and 1:15 make wise men into judges of Israel, and they are the KJV’s account of how a people that had one leader came to have many. “respect persons in judgment” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Deuteronomy 1:17, which is also the source of the appellate provision behind Mosiah 29:28.
provenance.significance: Moses at Deuteronomy 1:9 says “I am not able to bear you myself alone” and delegates; Mosiah at 29:11 delegates without the excuse, while still alive and competent, and permanently. The Mosaic precedent is for a judiciary that relieves a single leader, and the leader remains at its head. What Mosiah does with the same machinery is remove the head, which is why 29:29 has to invent something Deuteronomy does not have (see the row at 29:28).

29:11.note: “We will appoint wise men to be judges, that will judge this people according to the commandments of God.” The verbal contact is thin — two very common words — but the act is the specific act the KJV narrates twice, in Exodus 18 and Deuteronomy 1, and Mosiah’s chapter goes on to reproduce that passage’s appellate structure at 29:28 and its charge-formula at 29:30. Recorded here so that the reader meets the Mosaic precedent at the verse that enacts it.
29:11.whyNot: “Wise men” as judges is a natural English phrase and 42 KJV verses contain it. Nothing in 29:11 reproduces Deuteronomy 1 and the link would not stand at all if the surrounding verses did not carry the rest of the passage.
29:11.text: Take you wise men, and understanding, and known among your tribes, and I will make them rulers over you.

provenance.other: “should be judged of” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Corinthians 4:3, and it occurs there inside the identical antithesis: to be judged of man on one side and “he that judgeth me is the Lord” (4:4) on the other. Two Old Testament verses stand behind the thought without supplying the words: “take heed what ye do” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Chronicles 19:6 — “ye judge not for man, but for the LORD”, the charge Jehoshaphat gives the judges he sets in the land — and “the judgment is God” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Deuteronomy 1:17. mediation-check.py was run on Psalm 19:9 against Revelation 16:7 and 19:2 for the second half of the verse (“the judgments of God are always just” against “true and righteous are thy judgments”) and found no decisive divergence; the Book of Mormon reproduces neither form, so that clause cannot settle its own mediation.
provenance.significance: The KJV’s wording is what makes the sentence available. 1 Corinthians 4:3 renders Paul’s “human day” as “man’s judgment”, and it is that translator’s choice — not the Greek — that produces a clean English antithesis between being judged of God and being judged of man. Mosiah’s argument for a judiciary rests on the antithesis the King James translators created. The metalepsis is sharper still: Paul is refusing to let a congregation sit in judgment on him, and the ground of his refusal is that a human tribunal is not the tribunal that matters. Mosiah borrows the refusal in order to build a human tribunal with it, and 29:29 will end by letting the people judge their judges after all.

29:12.note: “Now it is better that a man should be judged of God than of man, for the judgments of God are always just, but the judgments of man are not always just.” The four-word run is a KJV singleton and it comes out of the one New Testament passage that argues the same antithesis in the same direction. Behind it, and supplying the setting rather than the words, is Jehoshaphat’s charge at 2 Chronicles 19:6 — the only place in the KJV where a king institutes judges and tells them whose judgment they are exercising. This chapter reaches that passage again at 29:30 and, structurally, at 29:42.
29:12.text: But with me it is a very small thing that I should be judged of you, or of man’s judgment: yea, I judge not mine own self.

provenance.other: “them that put their trust in him” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Proverbs 30:5 — a seven-word run reproduced without alteration. The near-parallels are not close: 2 Samuel 22:31 and Psalm 18:30 read “a buckler to all those that trust in him”, without “put” and without “them that”. mediation-check.py was run on all three and reported no decisive divergence, which is wrong on inspection — Mosiah plainly has “put their”, which Psalm 18:30 and 2 Samuel 22:31 lack. Decided by eye against the tool: the Book of Mormon has the Proverbs form.
provenance.significance: The half of Proverbs 30:5 that is not borrowed is “Every word of God is pure”, and the trust-formula is its consequent — the verse is about the reliability of what God has said. Mosiah 29 works entirely by a document: a written word sent among the people (29:4), more things written (29:33), and a people who at 29:37 “were convinced of the truth of his words.” The one KJV verse that promises shelter to those who put their trust in him promises it on the ground of a trustworthy word, in a chapter whose whole instrument is one.

29:20.note: “Extending the arm of mercy towards them that put their trust in him.” Seven words, verbatim, from the only KJV verse that contains them, and the near-misses in 2 Samuel and Psalms differ in exactly the words that would have made them candidates. The clause the phrase hangs on — the extended arm of mercy — is not from the KJV at all but is this book’s own formula (see the exclusion at this verse), which is what makes the Proverbs half of the sentence stand out.
29:20.text: Every word of God is pure: he is a shield unto them that put their trust in him.

provenance.route: 2 Chronicles 7:14 with Jonah 3:8 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: Two singletons in one sentence: “humble themselves” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Chronicles 7:14, and “cry mightily” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Jonah 3:8. Mosiah 29:20 has both, in the order the sources give them — humbling, then crying, then deliverance — with 29:19’s “sincere repentance” standing where Jonah 3:8 has “let them turn every one from his evil way” and 2 Chronicles 7:14 has “turn from their wicked ways”.
provenance.significance: Both sources are about deliverance granted to a people with no help from their king. 2 Chronicles 7:14 is God’s answer to Solomon at the dedication of the temple, and its conditions are laid on “my people”, not on the monarch; Jonah 3 is the one city in the Bible whose king can do nothing but put on sackcloth with everybody else. Mosiah cites them of Limhi’s and Alma’s people in bondage — people whose kings were the cause of the bondage — and the point of the citation is the argument of the whole chapter: what saved them was not the office. The verse then generalises it into a rule of providence, “thus doth the Lord work with his power in all cases among the children of men.”

29:20.note: “Because they did humble themselves before him; and because they cried mightily unto him, he did deliver them out of bondage.” Each phrase is a KJV singleton on its own; having both in one sentence, in sequence, with the repentance clause of 29:19 in front of them, is well past what coincidence covers. The two sources are unrelated to each other in the Bible and are fused here, which is the signature of composition out of remembered phrases rather than of quotation.
29:20.whyNot: Both phrases are short and each names an ordinary religious act; “humble themselves” in particular is a formula the Book of Mormon uses constantly, so its KJV rarity may say more about the KJV’s preference for “humble thyself” and “humbled himself” than about this verse’s source.
29:20.text: If my people, which are called by my name, shall humble themselves, and pray, and seek my face, and turn from their wicked ways; then will I hear from heaven, and will forgive their sin, and will heal their land.

provenance.route: Isaiah 32:1 → KJV → Book of Mormon; Matthew 7:6 for the second clause
provenance.other: “reign in righteousness” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 32:1. “trample them under” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 7:6, and “trample” in any form is in only three (Psalm 91:13, Isaiah 63:3, Matthew 7:6) — so the verb Mosiah chooses for what a king does to the commandments of God is a rare one, and the one KJV verse that uses it of contempt for something holy is the pearls-before-swine saying.
provenance.significance: Isaiah 32:1 is the KJV’s one promise of the good king — “Behold, a king shall reign in righteousness, and princes shall rule in judgment” — and Mosiah 29:22 makes the wicked king’s first act the tearing up of that king’s laws. The messianic guarantee is being cited as the thing a successor can destroy: righteousness reigned once and left statutes behind, and the next man repeals them. Isaiah’s promise is the premise of 29:13 (“if ye could have men for your kings, which would do even as my father Benjamin did”) and 29:16 is the refusal to build on it. If Matthew 7:6 is in the second clause, the commandments of God are the holy thing thrown to the swine.

29:22.note: “He teareth up the laws of those which have reigned in righteousness before him; and he trampleth under his feet the commandments of God.” The first phrase is a KJV singleton and it is the singleton about the ideal king; the second uses a verb the KJV reserves for three verses. Moderate rather than high because neither clause reproduces its source’s syntax — Isaiah has the future and a singular king, Mosiah a perfect and a plural — and because both phrases are short.
29:22.text: Behold, a king shall reign in righteousness, and princes shall rule in judgment.

provenance.other: Both halves of the Book of Mormon clause are KJV singletons and both are the same verse. “pervert the right ways of the Lord” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “enemy of all righteousness” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and Acts 13:10 is that verse in each case. Mosiah 29:23’s “doth pervert the ways of all righteousness” fuses them, taking the verb and object from one clause of Acts 13:10 and the “all righteousness” from the other; 29:7 has the first half plain, “perverting the way of the Lord”. The verse also holds two further rarities: “the manner of the king” occurs in exactly 3 KJV verses, all of them the Samuel passage this chapter is rewriting (1 Samuel 8:9, 8:11, 10:25), against Mosiah’s “laws after the manner of his own wickedness”; and “sent forth his armies” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 22:7, where an offended king destroys those who would not come.
provenance.significance: Two things follow from recovering Acts 13. The scene is a corrupt counsellor at a ruler’s elbow — Elymas beside Sergius Paulus — which is 29:22’s king who “hath his friends in iniquity, and he keepeth his guards about him”; and it ends with the ruler believing, as Mosiah’s people do at 29:37. More striking is what the same chapter of Acts contains eleven verses later: “and afterward they desired a king: and God gave unto them Saul” — “they desired a king” occurs in exactly one KJV verse — which is the New Testament’s only retelling of 1 Samuel 8. The chapter of the Bible that supplies Mosiah’s formula for a ruler who perverts righteousness is also the chapter that summarises the episode Mosiah 29 exists to reverse. Whether that is design or accident, it is worth the reader knowing.

29:23.note: “And thus an unrighteous king doth pervert the ways of all righteousness.” The sentence is built out of one KJV verse used twice: Acts 13:10 supplies both “pervert the … ways of the Lord” and “all righteousness”, each a singleton, and the Book of Mormon has welded them into a single predicate about kingship. That is more than a phrase in common; it is a small piece of composition on a source, and it is repeated in weaker form at 29:7. The 1830 and 1920 texts agree here, so the reading does not depend on the first edition.
29:23.text: And said, O full of all subtilty and all mischief, thou child of the devil, thou enemy of all righteousness, wilt thou not cease to pervert the right ways of the Lord?

provenance.route: Deuteronomy 1:17 and Exodus 18:22-26 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “small as well as the great” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Deuteronomy 1:17, and so does “respect persons in judgment”. Neither is reproduced; the shared thing is the appellate machinery, and the KJV builds it in exactly two places — Exodus 18:22 (“every great matter they shall bring unto thee, but every small matter they shall judge”) and Deuteronomy 1:17 (“the cause that is too hard for you, bring it unto me”).
provenance.significance: This is the chapter’s one genuinely unbiblical move, and it is made in biblical vocabulary. Jethro’s pyramid and its Deuteronomic restatement exist to route hard cases upward and end at one man; nothing in the KJV provides for judging the man at the top, because Moses is the top. Mosiah keeps the upward appeal at 29:28 — “ye can cause that they may be judged of a higher judge” — and then at 29:29 turns the structure over: “a small number of your lower judges” shall be gathered to judge the higher, “according to the voice of the people.” The apex is made answerable to the base. Deuteronomy 1:17’s ground for hearing the small as well as the great is that “the judgment is God” — a phrase that occurs in exactly one KJV verse — and Mosiah has already used that principle at 29:12. He then draws from it a conclusion Deuteronomy does not: if judgment belongs to God rather than to the office, the office can be reviewed from below.

29:28.note: “Ye can cause that they may be judged of a higher judge.” No wording of Exodus 18 or Deuteronomy 1 survives into the verse, so this is a figural link and is offered as one; what recommends it is that 29:11 has already appointed the wise men of Deuteronomy 1:13, 29:12 has already argued from Deuteronomy 1:17’s principle, and 29:30 will close with 2 Chronicles 19:9’s charge-formula. The Mosaic judiciary is demonstrably in the chapter; this is the verse where the Book of Mormon departs from it, and the departure is the finding.
29:28.whyNot: A tiered appeal is what any working court system needs and does not have to be borrowed from anywhere. The verse shares no distinctive language with either source, and a reader could reasonably hold that the Mosaic material is present in the chapter without being present in this verse.
29:28.text: Ye shall not respect persons in judgment; but ye shall hear the small as well as the great; ye shall not be afraid of the face of man; for the judgment is God’s: and the cause that is too hard for you, bring it unto me, and I will hear it.

provenance.other: “judge righteous judgment” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 7:24, where it is an imperative. Mosiah has it twice in this chapter, both times as the standard against which a judge is measured — 29:29’s “if your higher judges doth not judge righteous judgments” and 29:43’s “he did judge righteous judgments” of Alma — and pluralises the object, which the KJV never does with this phrase.
provenance.significance: John 7:24 is spoken in a quarrel about whether the men who administer the law keep it: five verses earlier, “Did not Moses give you the law, and yet none of you keepeth the law?” The Nephite constitution takes Jesus’s rule for judging a case and makes it the test for removing a judge from office — an ethical imperative converted into a procedural standard, and then applied at 29:43 to Alma, who holds the judgeship and the high priesthood together. The clause that supplies the criterion comes from a scene in which the priestly authorities are the ones failing it.

29:29.note: “If your higher judges doth not judge righteous judgments … they shall judge your higher judges, according to the voice of the people.” A KJV singleton doing constitutional work: the removal standard for a Nephite judge is a phrase that exists in one verse of the English Bible. Adjudicated here rather than at 29:43 because this is its first occurrence in the chapter; the 1830 keeps the non-standard concord “judges doth” which 1920 corrected to “do”, a change that touches the grammar and not the borrowing.
29:29.text: Judge not according to the appearance, but judge righteous judgment.

provenance.other: Three singletons from four consecutive verses. “ye do in the fear of the” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Chronicles 19:9 (“Thus shall ye do in the fear of the LORD”), against Mosiah’s “to do these things in the fear of the Lord”; “take heed what ye do” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 19:6; “set judges in the land” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 19:5. The n-gram stream instead proposed Deuteronomy 11:22 here on “I command you to do”, which is connective boilerplate and is filed in the exclusion register.
provenance.significance: 2 Chronicles 19:5-11 is the only narrative in the KJV of a king instituting a system of judges throughout his land, and every structural element of Mosiah 29 is in it. Jehoshaphat sets judges city by city (19:5, Mosiah 29:11, 29:41); he charges them that they judge not for man but for the LORD (19:6, Mosiah 29:12); he places priests and Levites over the appellate cases (19:8, Mosiah 29:28-29); he tells them to do it in the fear of the LORD (19:9, this verse); and he puts a chief priest over all matters of the LORD alongside a civil ruler for the king’s matters (19:11, and Mosiah 29:42’s Alma, who is given both). The difference is the one that matters: Jehoshaphat’s judges answer to Jehoshaphat, and after 29:30 the Nephite judges answer to nobody but each other and the people. Mosiah reproduces the biblical reform and removes its king, which is why the same verse that borrows the charge-formula also contains “that ye have no king”.

29:30.note: “And I command you to do these things in the fear of the Lord … and that ye have no king.” The charge-formula is a KJV singleton, and it belongs to the one royal judicial reform the Bible narrates — a passage whose other three verses this chapter has also been drawing on, at 29:12 and again at 29:42. That a single sentence carries both the borrowed charge and the abolition of the office that gave the charge is the chapter in miniature.
29:30.text: And he charged them, saying, Thus shall ye do in the fear of the LORD, faithfully, and with a perfect heart.

provenance.other: “upon their own heads” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Ezekiel 11:21. mediation-check.py was run on Ezekiel 11:21 against Ezekiel 33:4, Acts 18:6 and 1 Kings 2:32 and reported a decisive result for Ezekiel 33:4; that is an alignment artifact, produced by matching the tool’s “head” inside the Book of Mormon’s “heads”. Decided by eye, the case is not close: Mosiah has the plural noun and the third-person plural possessive, which is Ezekiel 11:21’s exact four words, where Ezekiel 33:4 and 1 Kings 2:32 read “his own head” and Acts 18:6 “your own heads”. CONVENTIONS §4’s warning about pronouns applies to number as well.
provenance.significance: In Ezekiel the formula is God’s and the recompense is eschatological: “I will recompense their way upon their own heads.” Mosiah legislates it. What the prophet says God will do at the end, the constitution arranges for now — which is why the next verse has to supply the corollary, that under a king the arrangement fails and “their iniquities are answered upon the heads of their kings”. Behind both stands Ezekiel 18:20, whose doctrine that the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father is here used, unusually, as an argument about political structure rather than about individuals: monarchy is objectionable because it makes one head bear a nation’s account, and 29:38’s “every man expressed a willingness to answer for his own sins” is the people accepting Ezekiel 18’s terms as a form of government.

29:30.note: “That if these people commit sins and iniquities, they shall be answered upon their own heads.” Four words from the only KJV verse that has them, in the right number and the right person, and doing at 29:30-31 exactly the theological work Ezekiel 18 does — which is what raises this above a lucky match on a common idiom. The verb is not Ezekiel’s (“recompense” becomes “answered”), so this is an allusion and not a quotation.
29:30.text: But as for them whose heart walketh after the heart of their detestable things and their abominations, I will recompense their way upon their own heads, saith the Lord GOD.

provenance.other: “live and inherit the land” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Deuteronomy 16:20, and the Book of Mormon reproduces it whole: “that we may live and inherit the land”. The same short passage yields two further singletons — “judges and officers” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Deuteronomy 16:18, and “which is altogether just” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 16:20 — and the liberty language of the verse has its own: “liberty throughout all the land” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Leviticus 25:10, the jubilee, which likewise returns every man to his possession. This is the chapter’s single longest verbatim run and the machine found it.
provenance.significance: Deuteronomy 16:18-20 is the Torah’s law for appointing judges, and 16:20 is the promise attached to obeying it: follow what is altogether just, “that thou mayest live, and inherit the land which the LORD thy God giveth thee.” Mosiah’s peroration on a land of liberty closes with that clause, in a chapter whose whole business is appointing judges — so the reward the KJV attaches to a judiciary is the reward Mosiah attaches to his. Two texts, separated by everything, agree that what a people gets for judging justly is tenure of its land. The KJV sequence is also the chapter’s sequence: 16:18 appoint judges (Mosiah 29:11, 29:25), 16:19 take no gift (29:40, the king who did not exact riches), 16:20 and you shall keep the land (here). The 1830 preserves “seeth” and “remaineth” where 1920 prints “sees” and “remains”, so the first edition sits closer to the source’s register than the modern text does.

29:32.note: “That we may live and inherit the land; yea, even as long as any of our posterity remaineth upon the face of the land.” Five words reproduced exactly from the one KJV verse that contains them, and that verse is the conclusion of the Bible’s law about appointing judges. Of everything in this chapter this is the cleanest case: the rarest run, from the most contextually apt source, at the rhetorical summit of Mosiah’s argument. It is well below Skousen’s sixteen-word threshold and is not one of his passages; the count is what carries it.
29:32.text: That which is altogether just shalt thou follow, that thou mayest live, and inherit the land which the LORD thy God giveth thee.

provenance.other: “travail of his soul” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 53:11, and “travail of” in any continuation occurs in exactly one KJV verse as well. The mediation cannot be settled by divergence, because there is no divergence to test: Mosiah 14 transcribes Isaiah 53 continuously and Mosiah 14:11 reproduces Isaiah 53:11 word for word. It is decided instead on proximity — the phrase re-enters the book fifteen chapters after the book itself has put it on the page, in the same authorial hand, which is the situation CONVENTIONS §7 has OT-via-earlier-BoM for. A reader who prefers direct-OT here is not making an error, only a different judgment about what ‘proximate model’ means when the two candidates are textually identical.
provenance.significance: The Servant’s travail is transferred to the office of a righteous king — and then, in the very next verse, refused. Isaiah 53:11 promises that the righteous servant “shall bear their iniquities”; Mosiah 29:34 answers that “the burdens should come upon all the people, that every man might bear his part”, and 29:30 has just legislated that sins are answered on the heads of those who commit them. So the chapter names the good king as a suffering servant in order to argue that nobody should be asked to be one. The substitution that is redemptive in Isaiah 53 is, as a political arrangement, precisely what Mosiah is abolishing. That reading is only available if the Isaiah is heard, which is what the singleton makes possible; compare Hays on metalepsis, where the meaning lies in what the two texts do not say to each other.

29:33.note: “All the travails of soul for their people”, said of a righteous king. The phrase belongs to one KJV verse, and this book has already printed that verse verbatim at Mosiah 14:11 as part of Abinadi’s Isaiah 53. Mosiah pluralises it and drops the possessive, which is how a remembered phrase behaves rather than a copied one. The argument for the row is not the two words but what 29:34 immediately does with them.
29:33.text: He shall see of the travail of his soul, and shall be satisfied: by his knowledge shall my righteous servant justify many; for he shall bear their iniquities.

provenance.route: Galatians 6:2 and 6:5 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “shall bear his own burden” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Galatians 6:5. mediation-check.py was run on Ezekiel 18:20 against Galatians 6:5 and 6:2 and found no decisive divergence — correctly, since the Book of Mormon reproduces none of the three verbatim. Decided on vocabulary instead: the words Mosiah shares (“burdens”, “every man”, “bear”) are Galatians’, and Ezekiel supplies only the doctrine, so mediation is direct-NT with Ezekiel 18 as a composite.
provenance.significance: Galatians 6:2 and 6:5 are the KJV’s famous unresolved pair — bear ye one another’s burdens, and every man shall bear his own burden — and Mosiah 29:34 holds both at once: the burdens fall on all the people, and each man carries his part of them. What is a puzzle in Paul is a constitutional principle here. Note the 1830 reading (CONVENTIONS §8): the first edition has “burdens” plural, which is Galatians 6:2’s form, and 1920 prints “burden” singular, which is 6:5’s. Whichever way the change is read, both readings are the KJV’s, and the modern text has moved from one verse of Galatians 6 to its neighbour.

29:34.note: “The burdens should come upon all the people, that every man might bear his part.” Galatians 6:5 is the only KJV verse with the construction, and Mosiah 29 has just spent four verses on the doctrine that Galatians 6:5 and Ezekiel 18:20 share — that accounts are individual and not transferable, which is the reason given for having no king. The substitution of “his part” for “his own burden” is what keeps this an allusion; the sentence is Paul’s two maxims combined rather than either one quoted.
29:34.text: For every man shall bear his own burden.

provenance.route: 1 Samuel 8:3, with the pastoral “filthy lucre” verses → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “lucre” occurs in exactly 6 KJV verses, and the distribution is the whole argument. Five are the qualification for a church officer — 1 Timothy 3:3 and 3:8, Titus 1:7 and 1:11, 1 Peter 5:2, all “filthy lucre” — and the sixth is 1 Samuel 8:3, of Samuel’s sons: “his sons walked not in his ways, but turned aside after lucre, and took bribes, and perverted judgment.” Separately, “exacted” occurs in exactly 2 KJV verses, 2 Kings 15:20 and 23:35, both of kings taking money of their people, against Mosiah’s “he had not exacted riches of them”.
provenance.significance: 1 Samuel 8:3 is the cause of the whole episode: Israel asks for a king because the judges have gone after lucre. Mosiah 29 ends by praising the last king for not going after lucre, and then — two verses later — installs judges. The KJV’s one non-ecclesiastical “lucre” names the exact failure that made monarchy look necessary, in the chapter that undoes the monarchy by restoring the office that failed. Read with the other five verses, the sentence is stranger still: the vocabulary in which Mosiah is cleared of avarice is the vocabulary in which the KJV screens candidates for the office of bishop and elder, and 29:42 immediately makes Alma chief judge and high priest at once. The two halves of the KJV’s “lucre” — the corrupt judge and the disqualified bishop — are the two halves of the office this chapter creates.
provenance.alternative: The five pastoral verses alone would account for the word, in which case the mediation is direct-NT and the significance is only that a civil ruler is measured by an ecclesiastical standard. That reading is weaker only because it has to ignore how thoroughly 1 Samuel 8 governs the rest of the chapter.

29:40.note: “They did not look upon him as a tyrant, who was seeking for gain, yea, for that lucre which doth corrupt the soul.” One word, and six KJV verses have it — which is why this is moderate and not high. The case is not the count but the split: one of the six is the verse that causes Israel to demand a king, in a chapter that has been rewriting that demand from its second verse, and the other five legislate the office Alma is about to receive alongside the judgeship. The nearest supporting rarity is “exacted”, whose only two KJV occurrences are both of kings extracting money from their subjects.
29:40.whyNot: A single content word cannot establish dependence, and “lucre” is simply the KJV’s word for ill-got money; a writer steeped in the English Bible would produce it without any particular verse in mind. The distributional argument is suggestive rather than demonstrative, and a cautious editor would decline it. It is written up because CONVENTIONS §0a asks for the risk to be taken openly.
29:40.text: And his sons walked not in his ways, but turned aside after lucre, and took bribes, and perverted judgment.

provenance.other: “chief priest is over you” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Chronicles 19:11, and “ruler of the house of Judah” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, the same one. Neither is reproduced, so this row is figural and stands on the arrangement rather than the words.
provenance.significance: Jehoshaphat’s reform ends by naming two men: Amariah the chief priest over all matters of the LORD, and Zebadiah the civil ruler for all the king’s matters. The Book of Mormon collapses them into one person in a single sentence — “Alma was appointed to be the chief judge; he being also the high priest” — at the end of a chapter that has taken the charge-formula (29:30), the not-for-man principle (29:12) and the city-by-city appointment (29:41) from the same eleven verses of 2 Chronicles. Where the biblical reform separates the sacred and civil apexes under a king, the Nephite one fuses them and removes the king. That is a structural inversion of a specific passage and it is worth recording as such, whatever a reader concludes about dependence.

29:42.note: “Alma was appointed to be the chief judge; he being also the high priest.” The double office is the chapter’s last constitutional act and it has an exact biblical counterpart, in the passage this chapter has already used three times: 2 Chronicles 19 divides the two offices between two named men, and Mosiah 29 unites them in one. Proposed as a figural link because there is no shared wording at all; its warrant is the accumulation of contact with 2 Chronicles 19:5-11 elsewhere in the chapter, and it should be withdrawn if that contact is judged to fail.
29:42.whyNot: No verbal contact whatever, and the Book of Mormon has its own reasons for the fusion — Alma is high priest because his father made him so (Mosiah 26:8), which the verse itself says. A reader may hold that the priest-and-judge arrangement of Mosiah 29:42 is fully explained by Mosiah 25-26 and owes 2 Chronicles nothing.
29:42.text: And, behold, Amariah the chief priest is over you in all matters of the LORD; and Zebadiah the son of Ishmael, the ruler of the house of Judah, for all the king’s matters: also the Levites shall be officers before you. Deal courageously, and the LORD shall be with the good.
